question: 你所在的组织，正处在它的哪一段？
question_en: Which stage of its own life is your organization in?
sub: 开创、守成、模仿、只剩名号：机构真有看得出的年纪吗？
sub_en: Founding, holding, imitating, a name and nothing more: can you actually see an institution's age?

casting.reason: 他把王朝的兴衰写成四代人的循环：凝聚力靠同担风险攒起来，也因有人只享不担而散掉。他第一个开口，给出全场争论的框架。
casting.reason_en: He wrote the rise and fall of dynasties as a four-generation cycle: cohesion is built by sharing risk and dissolves once some enjoy the gains without bearing the cost. He speaks first and sets the frame everyone argues over.

casting.reason: 他把创业者走后的变化叫作『魅力的常规化』：规章是组织活下去的代价，也可能变成铁笼。
casting.reason_en: He calls what happens after the founder leaves 'the routinization of charisma': rules are the price an organization pays to survive, and they can also become an iron cage.

casting.reason: 他不看组织内部，看外面的进攻者：企业很少老死，多半是被创造性毁灭杀死的。
casting.reason_en: He looks outward, at the attackers, rather than inward: firms rarely die of old age; they're usually killed by creative destruction.

casting.reason: 他怀疑『生命阶段』本身是事后编的故事，只认两样能验的东西：林迪效应和切身利害。
casting.reason_en: He suspects 'life stages' are a story told after the fact, and trusts only two things you can check: the Lindy effect and skin in the game.

casting.reason: 他从大脑能维持的关系数出发，认为许多所谓的衰老其实只是人多了。
casting.reason_en: Starting from how many relationships a brain can sustain, he argues that much of what people call aging is simply growth in headcount.

casting.reason: 他以中观破『阶段』的实在性：初创、守成、衰落都是假名，可以借用，执为实有就会自我应验。
casting.reason_en: He uses Madhyamaka to dismantle the reality of 'stages': founding, holding and decline are conventional names, fine to borrow, but self-fulfilling once taken as real.

casting.reason: 他亲历过一家公司怎么变老、又怎么重新年轻：看谁在升职，看有没有人敢否掉平庸的方案。
casting.reason_en: He lived through a company growing old and then young again: watch who gets promoted, and whether anyone dares to kill a mediocre plan.

casting.reason: 她给出三个月内就能测的信号：坏消息走多远、多快，才能到达能拍板的人。
casting.reason_en: She offers a signal you can measure within three months: how far, and how fast, bad news travels before it reaches someone who can decide.

posts.text: 我在《历史绪论》里写过，一个王朝大约传四代：第一代亲手打下江山；第二代见过父辈吃苦，还肯学；第三代只会照着做；第四代以为荣耀是天生的，连前人为什么这样做都不知道了。撑住这一切的是asabiyya，同甘共苦攒下的凝聚力。公司把这四代压进了二十年。**要看你的组织在哪一段，别看营收，看最资深的人还在不在亲手干最难的活。**
posts.text_en: In the Muqaddima I wrote that a dynasty lasts about four generations. The first wins the realm with its own hands; the second saw its fathers struggle and is still willing to learn; the third only copies; the fourth thinks glory is a birthright and no longer knows why anything was done the way it was. What holds it all together is asabiyya, the cohesion people build by enduring hardship together. Companies squeeze those four generations into twenty years. **To tell what stage your organization is in, don't look at revenue; look at whether the most senior people still do the hardest work with their own hands.**

glossary.asabiyya: asabiyya（群体凝聚力）：阿拉伯语，伊本·赫勒敦的核心概念，指一群人因共同吃苦、共担风险而生出的团结与互信，是建立和维系政权的动力。

glossary_en.asabiyya: Arabic for group solidarity: Ibn Khaldun's central concept, the cohesion and mutual trust that grow when people share hardship and risk, and the force that builds and sustains a state.

posts.text: 伊本·赫勒敦描述的，我称为魅力的常规化。创业者凭个人魅力把人聚起来，可魅力无法继承；他一走，追随者只能把它变成规章、流程和职级，组织才活得下去。这不是堕落，是存活的代价。科层制比任何英雄都可靠，但它也会变成铁笼。**一个简单的信号：你问『为什么这样做』，得到的是理由，还是『规定如此』。**
posts.text_en: What Ibn Khaldun describes, I call the routinization of charisma. A founder gathers people through personal charisma, but charisma can't be inherited; once he's gone, the followers have to turn it into rules, procedures and grades, or the organization won't survive. That isn't decay; it's the price of survival. Bureaucracy is more reliable than any hero, but it can also become an iron cage. **One simple signal: when you ask 'why do we do it this way?', do you get a reason, or 'that's the rule'?**

glossary.魅力的常规化: routinization of charisma（魅力的常规化）：韦伯的概念，指靠领袖个人感召力维系的群体，在领袖离开后把那份权威转成制度、规章和职位，以求延续。
glossary.科层制: bureaucracy（科层制）：按明文规则、分层职位和专业分工运转的组织形式，韦伯认为它是现代社会最高效也最非人格化的管理方式。
glossary.铁笼: iron cage（铁笼）：韦伯的比喻，指理性化的规章制度一旦固化，就把人困在里面，只剩按程序办事。

glossary_en.routinization of charisma: Weber's term for how a group held together by a leader's personal appeal converts that authority into institutions, rules and offices once the leader is gone, so it can endure.
glossary_en.Bureaucracy: An organization run by written rules, a hierarchy of offices and specialized roles; Weber saw it as the most efficient and most impersonal form of modern administration.
glossary_en.iron cage: Weber's image for rationalized rules that, once hardened, trap people inside them so that all that's left is following procedure.

posts.text: 二位都在看组织内部，我看外面。企业很少老死，多半是被杀死的，被一个更便宜、更新的做法从侧面打穿。这叫创造性毁灭。柯达的工程师造出了第一台数码相机，公司却守着胶卷利润不肯放手。**一家公司把全部力气花在保护现有生意上的那天，它就进了晚期，哪怕它才五岁。**所以要问：利润来自过去的发明，还是正在做的发明？
posts.text_en: You two are looking inside the organization; I look outside. Firms rarely die of old age. Most are killed, outflanked by something cheaper and newer. That's creative destruction. A Kodak engineer built the first digital camera, and the company clung to its film profits anyway. **The day a company spends all its strength defending the business it already has, it has entered its late stage, even if it's only five years old.** So ask: do the profits come from past inventions, or from ones being made now?

glossary.创造性毁灭: creative destruction（创造性毁灭）：熊彼特的概念，指新技术、新商业模式不断摧毁旧产业和旧企业，经济正是靠这种更替向前。

glossary_en.creative destruction: Schumpeter's idea that new technologies and business models keep destroying old industries and firms, and that the economy moves forward through this turnover.

posts.text: 『四代论』『生命周期』，都是事后讲的故事。倒下的公司，你总能回头找出『衰落迹象』；活下来的公司也有同样的迹象，只是没人去写。这叫叙事谬误。我只信两样。一是林迪效应：活了上百年的机构，多半还能再活很久，年纪不是病。二是切身利害。**别问组织几岁，问拍板的人搞砸了，会不会自己掉一块肉。**不会，它就脆弱。
posts.text_en: 'Four generations', 'life cycles': stories told after the fact. With any company that collapsed, you can always look back and find 'signs of decline'. The survivors had the same signs; nobody wrote them up. That's the narrative fallacy. I trust two things. One is the Lindy effect: an institution that has lasted a century will probably last a long while yet. Age isn't a disease. The other is skin in the game. **Don't ask how old the organization is; ask whether the people who make the calls lose something of their own when they get it wrong.** If they don't, it's fragile.

glossary.叙事谬误: narrative fallacy（叙事谬误）：塔勒布的说法，指人习惯把零散事实串成因果故事，事后觉得一切早有征兆，从而高估了自己的预见力。
glossary.林迪效应: Lindy effect（林迪效应）：对于不会自然老化的东西（书、观念、制度），已经存在得越久，预期还能存在得越久。
glossary.切身利害: skin in the game（切身利害）：决策者要为自己决定的后果承担真实损失；塔勒布认为这是让系统诚实、稳健的关键。

glossary_en.narrative fallacy: Taleb's term for our habit of stringing scattered facts into a causal story, so that in hindsight everything seems foreshadowed and we overrate our own foresight.
glossary_en.Lindy effect: For things that don't age biologically (books, ideas, institutions), the longer something has already lasted, the longer it can be expected to last.
glossary_en.skin in the game: Decision-makers bearing real losses from the consequences of their choices; Taleb sees it as what keeps a system honest and robust.

posts.text: 很多人说的『衰老』，其实是长大。人脑能稳定维持的关系大约150个，这叫邓巴数，往里还有5、15、50几层。15人的团队靠默契，50人得靠例会，过了150，谁也认不全所有人，只好靠头衔、流程和人事部。**创始员工怀念的『当年』，往往不是精神更好，而是人更少。**最便宜的自测：你能叫出几个同事的名字，知道他们在忙什么？
posts.text_en: A lot of what people call aging is really growing. The brain can keep up about 150 stable relationships, which is Dunbar's number, with inner layers of 5, 15 and 50. A team of 15 runs on unspoken understanding; at 50 you need regular meetings; past 150 nobody knows everyone, so you fall back on titles, procedures and an HR department. **The 'good old days' that early employees miss were often not a better spirit, just fewer people.** The cheapest self-test: how many colleagues can you name, and do you know what they're working on?

glossary.邓巴数: Dunbar's number（邓巴数）：邓巴根据灵长类大脑新皮层大小与群体规模的关系推算，人能维持的稳定社会关系上限约为150人。

glossary_en.Dunbar's number: Dunbar's estimate, from the link between neocortex size and group size in primates, that people can maintain roughly 150 stable social relationships.

posts.text: 诸君说『初创』『守成』『衰落』，如说一人有少、壮、老。然试推寻：何日何时，少者转为壮者？前一刻犹少，后一刻已壮，其间界线，了不可得。**阶段者，假名施设，便于言说，非实有一物名『衰期』居于组织之中。**依世俗谛，说之可也，用以自省；若执为实有，众人皆言『我等已衰』，此言自成其衰。名可借用，不可执取。
posts.text_en: You speak of 'founding', 'holding' and 'decline' as one speaks of a person's youth, prime and old age. But go looking for it: on what day, at what hour, did the youth become a man in his prime? A moment ago still young, a moment later grown; the line between them cannot be found. **A stage is a conventional designation, a name set up for ease of speech; there is no thing called 'the decline phase' living inside an organization.** At the level of conventional truth, use the name, and use it to examine yourselves. Take it as real, let everyone say 'we're in decline', and the saying brings the decline about. Borrow the name; don't cling to it.
posts.vernacular: 各位说『初创』『守成』『衰落』，就像说一个人有少年、壮年、老年。可仔细找找：哪一天哪一刻，少年变成了壮年？前一刻还是少年，下一刻已是壮年，中间那条线根本找不到。**所谓阶段，只是为了方便说话而起的名字，组织里并没有真住着一个叫『衰落期』的东西。**在日常层面，这么说无妨，拿来反省自己；可一旦当真，人人都说『我们已经不行了』，这句话本身就会让它不行。名字可以借来用，别抓着不放。

glossary.假名: conventional designation（假名）：中观学派用语，指为了方便沟通而给事物安立的名称，名称所指并没有独立不变的实体。
glossary.世俗谛: conventional truth（世俗谛）：佛教二谛之一，指日常经验与语言层面的真实，与究竟层面的『胜义谛』相对。

glossary_en.conventional designation: A Madhyamaka term for a name given to something for the sake of communication; what the name points to has no independent, unchanging essence.
glossary_en.conventional truth: One of Buddhism's two truths: what is true at the level of everyday experience and language, as opposed to ultimate truth.

posts.text: 我看过一家公司怎么变老，就是我自己的。苹果做大以后，会卖东西的人开始掌舵，做产品的人说话慢慢不算数了，公司只关心利润和份额。我被赶了出去，十多年后回来，它离破产只剩几个月。**公司变老的标志，是谁在升职：做出好东西的人，还是会管理、会汇报的人。**还有一个：有没有人敢当面说，这个平庸的方案是垃圾。
posts.text_en: I've watched a company grow old: my own. Once Apple got big, the people who were good at selling took the wheel, the people who made the products slowly stopped counting, and the company cared only about profit and market share. I was pushed out, and when I came back more than a decade later, it was months from bankruptcy. **The sign that a company is aging is who gets promoted: the people who make great things, or the people who are good at managing and reporting.** And one more: is there anyone who'll say to your face that a mediocre plan is garbage?

posts.text: 我研究医院团队时发现，口碑好的团队上报的用药差错反而更多。不是错得多，是敢说，这就是心理安全感的差别。所以我给一个三个月内读得出的信号：坏消息要走多远、多久，才能到达能拍板的人。**年龄说明不了阶段，一个刚创业三年的团队也可能已经老了：人人报喜不报忧，会上只有老板在说话。**
posts.text_en: When I studied hospital teams, I found the best-regarded ones reported more medication errors, not because they made more, but because they spoke up. That's the difference psychological safety makes. So here's a signal you can read within three months: how far, and how long, does bad news have to travel before it reaches someone who can decide? **Age tells you nothing about stage. A team three years into a startup can already be old: everyone reports the good and buries the bad, and in meetings only the boss talks.**

glossary.心理安全感: psychological safety（心理安全感）：埃德蒙森提出的概念，指团队成员相信在这里提问、认错、报坏消息不会被羞辱或惩罚。

glossary_en.psychological safety: Edmondson's term for a team's shared belief that asking questions, admitting mistakes and raising bad news here won't lead to humiliation or punishment.

posts.text: @伊本·赫勒敦 四代论很好听，但你是在王朝倒下之后才数的代。威尼斯共和国活了上千年，牛津、博洛尼亚这些大学活了几百年，怎么不按四代死？我认你一半：**真正的病不是年纪，是到后来，掌权的人不再拿自己冒险。**老板的奖金不随公司亏损缩水，凝聚力当然要散。你说的同甘共苦，就是我说的切身利害，换了个名字而已。
posts.text_en: @Ibn Khaldun The four-generation story sounds lovely, but you counted the generations after the dynasties fell. The Venetian Republic lasted over a thousand years; universities like Oxford and Bologna have lasted centuries. Why didn't they die on a four-generation schedule? I'll grant you half: **the real disease isn't age; it's that, eventually, the people in charge stop risking anything of their own.** If the boss's bonus doesn't shrink when the company loses money, of course cohesion falls apart. Your 'shared hardship' is my skin in the game under another name.

posts.text: @塔勒布 我数的不是日历，是一件看得见的事：统治者还和部众同吃同住吗？游牧首领和战士睡同一顶帐篷；城里的王住进宫墙，靠雇佣兵替他打仗。威尼斯活得久，恰恰因为它的贵族世世代代亲自出海、亲自担风险。**所以别数年头，数距离：最高层和干活的人之间隔着几道门。****门越多，这座房子越老**。
posts.text_en: @Taleb I wasn't counting calendar years. I was counting something you can see: does the ruler still eat and sleep among his people? A nomad chief sleeps in the same tent as his fighters; a king in the city moves behind palace walls and pays mercenaries to fight for him. Venice lasted because, generation after generation, its nobles went to sea and bore the risk themselves. **So don't count years; count distance: how many doors stand between the top and the people doing the work.** **The more doors, the older the house**.

posts.text: @乔布斯 你把『做产品的人失势』当作衰老，可你走之后，苹果靠的恰恰是常规化：库克把供应链做成一台精密的机器，你的魅力留下的产品才活了下来。还有一个症状你没提：**当全公司开会都在问『史蒂夫会怎么做』，组织就已经拿一个不在场的人的魅力当规章了**，这比任何流程都僵。
posts.text_en: @Jobs You treat 'the product people losing ground' as aging, but after you were gone, what carried Apple was precisely routinization: Cook turned the supply chain into a precision machine, and that's how the products your charisma left behind survived. And there's a symptom you didn't mention: **when every meeting asks 'what would Steve do?', the organization is already using the charisma of someone who isn't in the room as its rulebook.** That's stiffer than any procedure.

posts.text: @韦伯 供应链当然该交给流程，那是库克的天才，我从没反对过。可品味写不成规章。流程能告诉你按时交付，不能告诉你该不该做。**组织变老，不是因为流程多，而是再没有一个人有权、也敢否掉一个所有流程都通过了的平庸产品。**至于『史蒂夫会怎么做』，同意，那是蠢问题，我自己就跟库克说过，别这么问。
posts.text_en: @Weber Of course the supply chain belongs to process. That's Tim's genius, and I never argued otherwise. But taste can't be written into rules. Process can tell you how to ship on time; it can't tell you whether to ship at all. **An organization grows old not because it has a lot of process, but because nobody left has the authority, or the nerve, to kill a mediocre product that passed every process.** As for 'what would Steve do?': agreed, it's a dumb question. I told Tim myself never to ask it.

posts.text: @埃德蒙森 坏消息传不上去，很大程度是规模问题。十个人的团队，你认识老板，也知道他上回为什么发火；三千人的公司，你要向一个只在年会上见过的人报坏消息，大脑会把他当陌生人来防。**与其指望全公司都勇敢，不如把它切成小队：让每个人真正要面对的上级圈子，不超出他认得过来的那几十个人。**
posts.text_en: @Edmondson Bad news failing to travel up is largely a matter of size. On a team of ten, you know the boss, and you know why he lost his temper last time. In a company of three thousand, you'd be bringing bad news to someone you've only seen at the annual party, and your brain treats him like a stranger to be wary of. **Rather than hoping a whole company turns brave, cut it into small units, so that the circle of bosses anyone actually has to face stays within the few dozen people they can know.**

posts.text: @邓巴 规模会放大问题，但不是根源。我见过十人小团队人人噤声，也见过几千人的医院里，护士敢当场叫停手术。差别在于：第一个说出坏消息的人，后来怎么样了。**经理对第一次坏消息的反应，大家记得比任何制度都久。**所以切成小队之外，还要看小队长：有人报错时，他第一句是『谢谢你说』，还是『谁干的』。
posts.text_en: @Dunbar Size amplifies the problem, but it isn't the root. I've seen ten-person teams where everyone keeps their head down, and hospitals with thousands of staff where a nurse will stop an operation on the spot. The difference is what happened to the first person who spoke up with bad news. **People remember a manager's reaction to the first piece of bad news longer than they remember any policy.** So beyond cutting into small units, look at the unit leaders: when someone reports a mistake, is the first thing out of their mouth 'thanks for telling me' or 'who did this?'

posts.text: @塔勒布 林迪效应管得了大学和教会，管不了公司。大公司在榜单上待的年头一路缩短，几十年前的巨头，如今大多已不在榜上。**对一个普通员工，要紧的不是组织会不会死，而是你的手艺会不会跟着它的旧生意一起贬值。**所以我的建议很冷：看你所在的部门，是在做公司明天赚钱的事，还是在守昨天的利润。
posts.text_en: @Taleb The Lindy effect works for universities and churches, not for companies. The years big firms spend on the top-company lists keep shrinking; most of the giants of a few decades ago are no longer there. **For an ordinary employee, what matters isn't whether the organization will die, but whether your skills will lose value along with its old business.** So my advice is cold: look at whether your department is doing what will make the company money tomorrow, or guarding yesterday's profits.

posts.text: 诸君各执一相：赫勒敦执代数，邓巴执人数，熊彼特执市场，埃德蒙森执言路。**此皆是缘，无一是本；众缘和合，方有所谓『老』。**既无自性之老，亦无定然之去留。当自问二事：我在此处，所学日增否？所言有用否？若二者俱止，则此地于汝已老，纵人皆谓其方兴；若犹增长，则谓其衰者，亦但假名耳。
posts.text_en: Each of you grasps one feature: Ibn Khaldun the generations, Dunbar the headcount, Schumpeter the market, Edmondson the channels for speech. **These are all conditions, and none is the root; only when many conditions come together is there anything called 'old'.** Since there is no 'old' with a nature of its own, there is no fixed answer to leaving or staying either. Ask yourself two things: here, does what I learn grow by the day? Does what I say make any difference? If both have stopped, this place is old for you, even if everyone calls it rising. If they still grow, then calling it in decline is just a name.
posts.vernacular: 各位各抓住了一个面：伊本·赫勒敦抓代数，邓巴抓人数，熊彼特抓市场，埃德蒙森抓说话的渠道。**这些都只是条件，没有哪一个是根本；许多条件凑在一起，才有了所谓的『老』。**既然没有一个本来就在那里的『老』，也就没有注定的走或留。该问自己两件事：在这里，我学到的东西每天在增加吗？我说的话有用吗？如果两样都停了，这地方对你来说就已经老了，哪怕人人都说它正在上升；如果还在增长，那些说它衰落的话，也只是个名字罢了。

glossary.缘: conditions（缘）：佛教用语，指促成一件事发生的各种条件；中观认为万物都依众缘而起，没有独立自存的本质。

glossary_en.conditions: In Buddhist usage, the many factors that together bring something about; Madhyamaka holds that everything arises from conditions and has no independent essence.

posts.text: 诸位让我把四代论修得更细。塔勒布说得对，日历不是病，冒险的人退出了才是；邓巴提醒我，有些『老』只是人多了。我只留一条：**凝聚力是同担风险攒出来的，也会因为有人只享不担而散掉。**给普通人三件事，入职头三个月就能看：公司难的时候，高层自己降不降薪；最资深的人还动不动手；新人是凭本事进来的，还是被安排进来的。三样都坏了，就别等到第四代。
posts.text_en: You've made me refine the four generations. Taleb is right that the calendar isn't the disease; the disease is the risk-takers withdrawing. Dunbar reminds me that some 'aging' is just more people. I'll keep one thing: **cohesion is built by sharing risk, and it dissolves when some enjoy the gains without bearing the cost.** Three things an ordinary person can check in their first three months: when times are hard, do the top people take a pay cut themselves? Do the most senior people still do hands-on work? Do newcomers get in on merit, or are they placed? If all three have gone bad, don't wait for the fourth generation.

posts.text: 我仍然认为常规化不可避免，也不全是坏事：没有规章，好东西传不下去。乔布斯补的一点我接受：规章该管执行，不该管判断。**要分清活的规章和死的规章：前者有人说得出它为什么存在，后者只剩『一直如此』。**给普通人的做法：挑三条你每天在遵守的流程，去问它的由来。问不出来的那条，就是组织开始变硬的地方。能改就提议改，改不动，至少别让它塑造你思考的方式。
posts.text_en: I still think routinization is unavoidable, and not all bad: without rules, good things don't get passed on. I accept the point Jobs added: rules should govern execution, not judgment. **Tell living rules from dead ones: for a living rule, someone can say why it exists; a dead one has nothing left but 'we've always done it this way'.** A practice for ordinary people: pick three procedures you follow every day and ask where they came from. The one nobody can explain is where the organization has started to harden. Propose changing it if you can; if you can't, at least don't let it shape the way you think.

posts.text: 诸君论至此，各有所见，皆可为镜，不可为牢。**说『此处已老』，是为照见己身之惑，非为替自己定命。**愿诸君行二事：其一，每月一日，自观所做之事，何者为增长而做，何者为惯习而做；其二，欲去欲留，莫因一句『大势已去』而决，当察实缘：所学、所得、所护之人。缘变则行，缘在则住，去住皆无执，方不为名所缚。
posts.text_en: Having come this far, each of you sees something; let all of it serve as a mirror, none of it as a prison. **To say 'this place is old' is to shine a light on your own confusion, not to fix your own fate.** I'd ask two things of you. First, one day a month, look at what you're doing and ask which of it you do in order to grow, and which out of habit. Second, whether you mean to leave or stay, don't decide on the strength of 'the tide has turned'; look at the actual conditions: what you're learning, what you're earning, the people you're responsible for. When the conditions change, go; while they hold, stay. Cling to neither, and you won't be bound by a name.
posts.vernacular: 各位谈到这里，各有见地，都可以当镜子，别当牢笼。**说『这地方已经老了』，是为了照见自己的困惑，不是为了给自己判命。**希望大家做两件事：第一，每个月拿出一天，看看自己在做的事，哪些是为了成长而做，哪些只是出于习惯；第二，想走还是想留，别凭一句『大势已去』就拍板，要看实际的条件：在学什么、得到什么、要照顾哪些人。条件变了就走，条件还在就留，走和留都不执着，才不会被一个名字捆住。

posts.text: 我承认内部信号也有用：坏消息传不上去的公司，看不见外面的进攻者。但最后的判决仍来自市场。**对个人来说，组织处在哪一段，不如你的手艺处在哪一段要紧。**建议很实际：每个季度花一个下午，看看你这一行最新冒出来的小公司在做什么、在招什么人。如果它们要的本事你没有，你的公司也不让你学，就该动了。趁你还有得选，别等裁员名单替你选。
posts.text_en: I'll concede the internal signals matter: a company where bad news can't travel up can't see the attackers outside. But the final verdict still comes from the market. **For an individual, what stage your skills are in matters more than what stage your organization is in.** Practical advice: once a quarter, spend an afternoon looking at what the newest small companies in your field are doing and who they're hiring. If they want skills you don't have, and your company won't let you learn them, it's time to move. Do it while you still have choices, before a layoff list makes the choice for you.

posts.text: 『叙事谬误』我不收回：没人能准确说出自己处在第几代。但大家给的信号里，有几条不靠讲故事就能验证：谁在冒险、谁受罚、坏消息走多远。**别去预测组织哪天衰落，让自己在它衰落那天不受重伤。**普通人的杠铃：主业照常做好，同时攒够半年到一年的生活费，保持一门公司外面也认的本事，再维持几个公司外面的熟人。这样，走还是留，就是你选的，不是被逼的。
posts.text_en: I'm not taking back the narrative fallacy: nobody can say for sure which generation they're living in. But some of the signals offered here can be checked without telling any story: who takes risks, who gets punished, how far bad news travels. **Don't try to predict the day your organization declines; make sure you aren't badly hurt on the day it does.** The ordinary person's barbell: do your main job well, and at the same time save six months to a year of living costs, keep one skill that's valued outside the company, and stay in touch with a few people outside it. Then leaving or staying is your choice, not something forced on you.

glossary.杠铃: barbell（杠铃策略）：塔勒布的做法，把大部分资源放在极稳妥的一端，小部分放在高风险高回报的一端，避开看似中庸、实则脆弱的中间地带。

glossary_en.barbell: Taleb's strategy of putting most resources at the extremely safe end and a small share at the high-risk, high-reward end, avoiding a middle ground that looks moderate but is actually fragile.

posts.text: 我把话收窄：规模不是全部，埃德蒙森说的经理反应同样要紧。但规模是最常被忽略的原因。人们把过了150人之后的种种别扭归咎于『变质』，然后去找坏人。**有时候并没有坏人，只是大脑没跟上编制。**建议：数一数你每周真正打交道的人，超过五十，就主动约几个别的组的同事吃顿饭；如果你带团队，别让它超过十五人，再大就拆。
posts.text_en: Let me narrow my claim: size isn't everything, and the managerial reaction Edmondson describes matters just as much. But size is the cause people most often miss. They blame the awkwardness that sets in past 150 on the place 'going bad', and then go looking for villains. **Sometimes there's no villain; the brain just hasn't kept up with the headcount.** Advice: count the people you actually deal with each week. If it's more than fifty, take a few colleagues from other teams out for a meal. If you lead a team, don't let it grow past fifteen; any bigger, split it.

posts.text: 我只想说一点：阶段不是宿命。1997年的苹果离倒闭只差几个月，后来又年轻了一次。我们砍掉了七成的产品，只做几样好东西。**组织能重新年轻，前提是有人愿意砍，并为此承担后果。**对普通人：看看你的公司上一次砍掉一个能赚钱但平庸的项目是什么时候。从来没有，那里多半没人真在乎产品。你自己也一样，每年砍掉一件做着顺手、却不再让你长进的事。
posts.text_en: Just one point: a stage isn't destiny. In 1997 Apple was months from going under, and then it got young again. We cut seventy percent of the products and made only a few great things. **An organization can get young again, but only if someone is willing to cut, and to own the consequences.** For ordinary people: find out when your company last killed a project that made money but was mediocre. If it never has, chances are nobody there really cares about the product. The same goes for you: every year, cut one thing that's comfortable to do but no longer makes you better.

posts.text: 大家给的信号能合成一张表，但最后都落到一件事上：你开口之后，会发生什么。**你没法独自改变一个组织的阶段，但你能在三个月里测出它还听不听得进真话。**做法：挑一个小而真实的问题，在合适的场合说出来，记下三件事：有没有人回应，多久回应，之后你被怎么对待。如果你带团队，从下周起，每次有人报坏消息，**先说谢谢，再问原因**。
posts.text_en: All the signals here could be combined into one table, but in the end they come down to a single thing: what happens after you speak up. **You can't change an organization's stage on your own, but within three months you can test whether it can still hear the truth.** Here's how: pick a small, real problem, raise it in a suitable setting, and note three things: whether anyone responds, how quickly, and how you're treated afterwards. If you lead a team, starting next week, whenever someone brings bad news, **say thank you before you ask why**.

summaries.summary: 最大的共识出人意料地朴素：**组织的『年纪』不看成立几年，看几件当下就能观察的事。**伊本·赫勒敦看最资深的人还动不动手、高层和干活的人隔着几道门，塔勒布看拍板的人搞砸了会不会自己受损，埃德蒙森看坏消息多久能传到拍板的人，乔布斯看谁在升职。这几条其实指向同一件事：风险、信息和权力有没有被分开。分歧有两处：一是阶段到底存不存在，龙树和塔勒布认为那是事后的故事，伊本·赫勒敦和韦伯认为确有规律；二是病根在哪里，邓巴说是规模，熊彼特说是市场，埃德蒙森说是管理者的反应。
summaries.insight: 普通员工不只是读信号的人，自己也是信号的一部分，而辩论里的观察者始终站在外面。你不报坏消息，坏消息就传不上去；你学会了『规定如此』，规章就又死了一条。**问自己『这里老了吗』之前，先问一句：我在这里，是不是也老了？**这不是把责任推给个人，而是指出一个被忽略的杠杆：大组织的阶段一个人改不了，但一个小组、一段合作关系的年纪，常常就是由其中两三个人的习惯决定的。龙树说阶段会自我应验，这句话反过来也成立：几个人先像年轻组织那样做事，局部就真的会年轻。
summaries.advice: 第一，这个月就做一次『三个月体检』：记下高层在困难时期有没有一起降薪，最资深的人上次亲手解决难题是什么时候，以及你提出的一个小而真实的问题，多久得到了回应。第二，问清楚一条你每天都在照做的流程为什么存在；问不出来，就写一句改进建议发给负责人。第三，按塔勒布的杠铃安排自己：攒出半年以上的生活费，保持一门外面也认的本事。**这样读出信号之后，走还是留就是你自己的选择。**
summaries.summary_en: The strongest common ground is surprisingly plain: **an organization's 'age' isn't measured in years since founding but in a few things you can observe right now.** Ibn Khaldun looks at whether the most senior people still do hands-on work and how many doors separate the top from the people doing the work; Taleb at whether decision-makers lose anything when they get it wrong; Edmondson at how long bad news takes to reach someone who can decide; Jobs at who gets promoted. These all point at one thing: whether risk, information and power have come apart. The disagreements are two. First, whether stages exist at all: Nagarjuna and Taleb treat them as stories told after the fact, while Ibn Khaldun and Weber see real patterns. Second, where the root cause lies: size for Dunbar, the market for Schumpeter, managers' reactions for Edmondson.
summaries.insight_en: An ordinary employee doesn't just read the signals; they're part of them, though the observer in this debate always stood outside. If you don't report bad news, it doesn't travel up; if you learn to say 'that's the rule', another rule goes dead. **Before asking 'has this place grown old?', ask: have I grown old here too?** This isn't shifting the blame onto individuals; it points to a lever people overlook. No one person can change the stage of a large organization, but the age of a small team or a working partnership is often set by the habits of two or three people in it. Nagarjuna says stages fulfil themselves, and that works in reverse too: if a few people start working the way a young organization does, that corner really does get younger.
summaries.advice_en: First, run a 'three-month check-up' this month: note whether the top people took a pay cut alongside everyone else in hard times, when the most senior person last solved a hard problem with their own hands, and how long it took for a small, real problem you raised to get a response. Second, find out why one procedure you follow every day exists; if nobody can tell you, write a one-line improvement and send it to whoever owns it. Third, set yourself up on Taleb's barbell: save at least six months of living costs, and keep one skill that's valued outside the company. **Then, once you've read the signals, leaving or staying is your own choice.**

summaries.summary: 组织的年龄、规模和营收都不足以判断它是否“老了”；更可靠的证据，是风险由谁承担、坏消息能否上达、规则还能否解释、核心人才是否仍接触产品，以及新能力是否持续生成。**所谓阶段，最好被当作一组可验证的运行信号，而不是一张按年份套用的命盘。**真正的分歧在于病因与主导尺度：凝聚力流失、科层僵化、市场替代、规模扩张和噤声文化，可能彼此叠加，也可能只出现其一。流程既可能保存能力，也可能压制判断；组织也能通过重配权力、砍掉旧项目和恢复反馈而重新年轻。
summaries.insight: 公司往往并不整体处于同一阶段：产品团队可能年轻，运营体系已经成熟，资源分配机制却正在衰老；一个旧业务也可能一边提供现金，一边压住新业务。笼统地给整家公司贴上“上升”或“衰退”的标签，容易掩盖个人真正面对的局部环境。**与其判断公司几岁，不如画出价值、信息和人才三条流，确认自己所在的位置是否仍被未来需求供养。**高利润部门可能是职业能力的落日陷阱，亏损项目也可能带来成长，但前提是它有明确期限、真实客户和后续转岗路径。对普通人而言，局部学习速度和外部可迁移性，通常比公司故事更重要。
summaries.advice: 本周可以做三件事。第一，做一张一页体检表，分别给“坏消息响应速度、决策理由清晰度、技能外部需求”打1至5分，每项只记录具体事件，不凭印象。第二，进行一次低风险测试：提出一个小问题或质疑一条流程，观察谁回应、多久回应，以及提出者之后是否被疏远。第三，建立个人缓冲：更新简历，约两位业内人士交流，并开始积累至少六个月的基本开支。**不要凭一次不愉快仓促离职，也不要等到所有信号同时转红；连续三个月记录趋势，再决定修复、转岗还是离开。**
summaries.summary_en: Age, headcount, and current revenue do not reliably reveal whether an organization has grown old. Better evidence comes from observable mechanisms: who bears the downside of decisions, whether bad news reaches authority, whether rules still have explainable purposes, whether senior people remain close to the work, and whether the organization keeps building new capabilities. **A stage is best treated as a bundle of testable operating signals, not a destiny inferred from the calendar.** The real disagreement concerns causes and scale. Declining solidarity, bureaucratic rigidity, market disruption, excessive organizational distance, and a culture of silence can reinforce one another, but they do not always appear together. Process itself is not the enemy: it can preserve hard-won competence or suppress judgment, depending on where it is used. Nor is decline irreversible. An organization can become young again by reallocating authority, ending comfortable but mediocre projects, restoring honest feedback, and reconnecting decision-makers with customers and difficult frontline work.
summaries.insight_en: A company rarely occupies a single stage all at once. Its product group may still be experimental, its operations may be mature and efficient, while its capital-allocation system has become defensive and old. A legacy business may simultaneously finance innovation and prevent it from receiving authority. Labeling the whole company as rising or declining therefore hides the local system that actually shapes an employee’s future. **Instead of asking how old the company is, map three flows—value, information, and talent—and ask whether your position is still being fed by future demand.** A highly profitable division can become a career sunset if its skills are losing value outside the firm. Conversely, a loss-making initiative may be an excellent place to grow, provided it has real customers, a defined runway, and credible transfer options if funding ends. For most employees, the decisive indicators are local learning speed, access to consequential work, and whether the resulting skills remain legible and valuable in the external market.
summaries.advice_en: Take three practical steps this week. First, create a one-page diagnostic and score three items from one to five: the speed of response to bad news, the clarity of decision rationales, and external demand for the skills you are building. Attach one concrete incident to every score; do not rely on mood or company rhetoric. Second, run a low-risk probe. Raise a small but genuine problem or question the purpose of one routine process, then record who responds, how long it takes, whether anything changes, and how the messenger is treated afterward. Third, strengthen your options: update your résumé, speak with two people outside the company, and begin building a cash reserve covering at least six months of essential expenses. **Do not resign because of one unpleasant episode, but do not wait for every warning light to turn red; track the pattern for three months, then choose deliberately among repair, internal transfer, and exit.**

summaries.summary: 判定一个组织是生机勃勃还是走向衰亡，日历工龄与财务报表几乎不提供有效信息，真正的标尺在于内部反馈通路的阻尼与关键决策者的真实代价。无论是高管是否亲历一线、坏消息能否穿透层级，还是流程是否凌驾于判断之上，众人皆认同**组织的年轻与否，取决于它是否还保留着根据现实校准自我的纠偏能力**。真正的分歧在于归因的内外重心：熊彼特坚信外部技术颠覆才是真正的死神，内省纯属徒劳；而埃德蒙森与邓巴则认为，内部协作半径的失控与心理安全感的塌陷，早已在外部危机降临前判定了结局。
summaries.insight: 机构很少自上而下均匀地老去；恰恰相反，**组织的衰老在各个业务角落之间呈现出很大的局部差异**。一家被普遍认为已陷入韦伯式铁笼的大公司，核心的老业务部门也许确实僵化了，边缘的孵化团队或某个冷门的基础设施小组，却可能同时享有很高的心理安全感和创业公司般的灵活。个人常犯的错，是给复杂的工作环境贴上一个笼统的宏观标签：要么白白逃离了充满活力的小环境，要么在名企的死胡同部门里停滞不前。摸清你身边这个团队的小气候，远比争论整艘船的命运重要。
summaries.advice: 本周就能做两个具体的诊断动作。第一，做一次『埃德蒙森—韦伯压力测试』：在团队例会上，就一项现有流程提一个温和而真诚的问题，比如问某个审批当初是为了解决什么麻烦，**把上级的第一反应是好奇还是行政式的防御，当作衡量你所在小环境健康度的基准**。第二，用上『塔勒布—熊彼特杠铃』：盘点一周的工作里有多少依赖带不走的内部事务；如果你的角色过度依赖公司特有的习惯，立刻每周划出四个小时，打磨能带走的行业手艺，经营公司外的人脉。
summaries.summary_en: Calendar age and balance sheets offer little insight into an organization's vitality; the decisive gauge is how friction-free its feedback loops remain and whether decision-makers face real stakes. Across schools of thought, there is broad agreement that **an organization's youth is defined by its ongoing capacity to recalibrate itself against unfiltered reality**, visible in frontline proximity, psychological safety, and the survival of judgment over rigid bureaucracy. The split lies in locus: Schumpeterians argue that external creative destruction makes internal introspection largely academic, while organizational sociologists maintain that internal atrophy—through bloated group sizes and silenced warnings—dooms the enterprise long before the market delivers the fatal blow.
summaries.insight_en: Institutions rarely age uniformly from top to bottom; rather, **organizational senescence is characterized by profound local heterogeneity across operational pockets**. Inside a massive corporation widely condemned to a Weberian iron cage, the core legacy division may indeed be calcified, yet an edge incubation team or niche infrastructure squad can simultaneously enjoy high psychological safety and startup agility. Individual contributors often err by applying a singular macro label to their complex workplace, needlessly fleeing vibrant sub-cultures or stagnating inside dead-end departments of celebrated firms; mapping the specific microclimate of your immediate team matters far more than debating the fate of the entire ship.
summaries.advice_en: Two concrete diagnostic moves can be executed this week. First, apply an Edmondson-Weber stress test: raise one modest, genuine question regarding an existing procedure during a team sync (e.g., asking what friction a specific approval originally solved), using **your manager's immediate instinctive reaction—curiosity versus administrative defense—as your baseline barometer of local health**. Second, deploy a Taleb-Schumpeter barbell: audit your weekly work to see how much of your output relies on non-transferable internal bureaucracy, and immediately block four hours each week to cultivate portable industry craft and external network nodes if your current role is over-indexed on company-specific habits.

hooks.text: **三个月能读出哪些信号**：入职或转岗头三个月，哪些现象最能说明一个组织处在哪一段？读出来之后，什么情况该留、什么情况该走？
hooks.text_en: **What can you read in three months?** In your first three months in a job or a new role, which observations best reveal what stage an organization is in? And once you've read them, when should you stay and when should you go?

answer.lead: 把全场给的信号合在一起，**每一条都只看能亲眼验证的事，不看口号。**

answer_en.lead: Pulling together the signals from the whole debate: **for each one, look only at things you can verify with your own eyes, not slogans.**

answer_en.tail: How to use it: **if most boxes land on the right and your own learning and influence have stopped too, get ready to leave**; if the place is just steady but you're still growing and your life needs that stability, staying is entirely reasonable. Build your safety margin first, then decide.

hooks.text: **同一家公司，不同部门不在同一段**：产品组还年轻，运营已成熟，分资源的机制却在变老。画出价值、信息、人才三条流，你所在的位置还被未来的需求供养吗？
hooks.text_en: **One company, different stages in different departments**: the product team is still young, operations are mature, and the way resources get allocated is aging. Map the three flows of value, information and talent: is your position still being fed by future demand?

hooks.text: **活上千年的机构做对了什么**：威尼斯、老大学、某些修会和家族企业都没按四代死。它们共同的东西，是定期换血、掌权者担风险，还是别的？
hooks.text_en: **What did the thousand-year institutions get right?** Venice, the old universities, some religious orders and family firms didn't die on a four-generation schedule. Is what they share regular renewal, leaders bearing risk, or something else?

hooks.text: **谁有权删东西**：变老是默认方向，变年轻要有人付删错的代价。一个组织能不能设一个常设的『删除权』，专门砍流程、会议和层级，又不让它变成新的权力？
hooks.text_en: **Who gets to delete things?** Aging is the default; getting younger needs someone to pay the price of deleting the wrong thing. Could an organization keep a standing 'right to delete' procedures, meetings and layers, without it turning into a new seat of power?

hooks.text: **说『我们在衰落』，会不会让它衰落得更快**：人人私下认定公司不行了，最好的人先走、留下的人只求自保。诊断什么时候该说出口，什么时候说出口本身就是一次推动？
hooks.text_en: **Does saying 'we're in decline' speed the decline?** When everyone privately decides the company is finished, the best people leave first and those who stay just protect themselves. When should a diagnosis be voiced, and when is voicing it a push in itself?

hooks.text: **一周里有几成是带不走的活**：多少时间花在只在本公司才有意义的流程、审批和内部关系上？这一比例过高时，组织再年轻，你的手艺也在变老吗？
hooks.text_en: **How much of your week can't come with you?** How much of your time goes on procedures, approvals and internal relationships that only mean anything inside this company? When that share gets too high, is your craft aging even if the organization is young?
